speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INCLUSION OF SOIL
subsubtopic: IMPROVING CROPS IN SPECIFIED ACREAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the house of a change which will be made by the Canadian wheat board in the basis of the specified acreage upon which general delivery quotas are based. From time to time producers, farm organizations and others interested in land utilization in the prairie provinces have expressed the view that some encouragement should be given to individual producers to increase their acreages of soil improving forage crops. They believe that such a development in suitable areas within the prairie provinces would be constructive from the standpoint of the agricultural industry. It has been further indicated that a measure of encouragement would be accomplished if acreages seeded to such soil improving crops were included in the specified acreages upon which the board's general delivery quotas are based.
The wheat board has given careful consideration to this matter and thinks there is merit in including soil improving forage crops in its specified acreage, and this change will be effective for the 1957-58 crop year.
I might add that at the present time specified
acreage consists of acreage which producers seeded to wheat other than Durums, oats, barley, rye, and land in summer fallow. I believe that this change approved by the wheat board is a constructive one and in the long-range interests of western agriculture.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF SOIL
subsubtopic: IMPROVING CROPS IN SPECIFIED ACREAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of the statement that specified acreage for quota purposes will include forage crops. Is this policy being conducted to encourage a shift of acreage from grain to forage crops? Has any consideration been given to adopting a Canadian soil bank program?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INCLUSION OF SOIL
subsubtopic: IMPROVING CROPS IN SPECIFIED ACREAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the change in the basis for quotas was made at the request of farm organizations. The purpose was not to penalize those farmers who believe that soil building crops are the proper adjunct to their farming methods. There is no consideration being given at the moment to setting up a soil bank program such as the one recently adopted in the United States. [Later:]

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRASH AT ST. JAMES, MANITOBA

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Gordon Churchill (Winnipeg South
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of National Defence the following question. Will the minister give the house some information concerning the recent crash of an R.C.A.F. bomber near St. James, Manitoba?
Hen. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence): I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. While the press coverage of this accident was quite extensive, l might summarize the principal facts. On Sunday evening a Mitchell aircraft was returning to Stevenson field from a routine long-range training flight from Vancouver. As the aircraft approached for a normal landing it apparently ran into difficulty and lost height quite rapidly. It crashed in the built-up area of the city of St. James causing some damage to one house and two garages and coming to a halt against an unoccupied partially constructed house. There were five regular air force and one reserve force airmen on board and apart from minor injuries suffered by three of these personnel there were no other service or civilian injuries.
A full investigation has been ordered and until a report has been made I am unable to deal with the cause of the crash. Civilian claims for damage will of course be settled in the normal manner as soon as determined.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
It would, of course, be difficult and probably not appropriate for me to make a statement on the orders of the day on a matter of such general importance, and it would take a great deal of time. But I can tell my hon. friend that, as he knows, the general assembly of the United Nations was to have discussed the Middle East situation today. That discussion has been postponed until Thursday in order, among other things, to give the delegations a little longer to work out proposals which might be of some value when the assembly meets on Thursday in bringing about an agreed withdrawal of Israeli forces from the two parts of Egyptian or Egyptian-controlled territory which they now occupy.
It has been suggested that a sanctions resolution might be introduced for this purpose, and that this kind of pressure would be required, but I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we have reached that point yet. I think there is still a very good possibility of bringing about an agreed withdrawal by relating the necessity for withdrawal, which has already been indicated by assembly resolutions, with the equal necessity of ensuring that the withdrawal should not be to the state of affairs which existed last October, and which had so much to do with bringing about the explosion then.
I think those two objectives can be reconciled, and I think if they can the question of sanctions need not arise.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR CURRENT FIGURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked a question to which I promised a reply as soon as possible. He asked if I would make a statement regarding the unemployment situation in the country generally this winter.
I find that the latest information available and summarized in the regular monthly joint release of the dominion bureau of statistics and the economics and research branch of my department just went out yesterday reporting the situation as at January 19 last. This release goes into the matter at some length and I shall attempt to see that the hon. member for Kamloops or any other member in this house who may wish it receives a copy. In the meantime here are the highlights for Canada as a whole.

At January 19, 1957, the number of persons with jobs was estimated at 5,393,000, some
162,000	lower than at mid-December but still about 162,000 higher than in January a year ago. Persons without jobs and seeking work, according to the dominion bureau of statistics survey, rose to an estimated
303,000,	which was some 17,000 more than in January, 1956, and about 60,000 less than in January, 1955.
The increase this January over last comes primarily from such seasonal industries as construction, lumbering, logging and transportation. Bad weather and the effects of the C.P.R. strike all contributed to the lay-offs.
In this connection I think I should acknowledge and commend the vigorous and co-ordinated efforts now under way in many localities across Canada to increase winter employment opportunities. These steps are making a definite contribution to the maintenance of employment. Without them, unemployment this winter would be much higher than it is.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution which has just been read to the committee is on the order paper as a result of recommendations which have been made from time to time for amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I think it is correct to say that the first representations made in the house in recent years to this effect were made from both sides of the house in the session of 1955, and the recommendations then made were acted upon at that time but not to the full extent of those recommendations.
I would like to say, before discussing the intention of the amendments which were then made, that this act was placed on the statute books back in 1939 as a result of experiences which we had gone through in Canada for seven or eight years preceding that time. And I may say, too, that for 30 or 40 years before that time there had been strong recommendations by farm organizations in different parts of Canada to the effect that some form of crop insurance should be provided. But so far as I have been able to ascertain, no person or group of persons has been able to evolve a scheme of crop insurance which would cover all crops effectively. In addition, it was fairly well established in the earlier days, and established, I think, in the courts as well as otherwise, that insurance is a matter which can be dealt with by legislation only in the provinces. In order to strengthen that opinion I would call attention to the fact that when this measure was sent to the Senate in 1939 I was asked to attend before a committee of the other place. At that time there was a very well known and well qualified legal authority there in the person of Mr. Arthur Meighen. When the bill was brought before that committee he asked me the direct question: Is this crop insurance or is it insurance? I said, "My legal advisers tell me it is not." He said that if it were it would not be possible for the federal parliament to pass the legislation but he wanted it to be understood that, if the legislation were within the powers of the federal parliament, he thought it was the kind of legislation which under the circumstances was greatly needed.
But he indicated that he was not prepared to accept just the opinion of the legal advisers of my department and he asked for the opinion of the then legal adviser of the other place who was also a very well known and very well qualified legal authority. The then legal adviser to the Senate indicated to the committee that in his opinion this measure

was not insurance. On the strength of that Mr. Meighen advised that he would favour the legislation and so did the other members of the Senate committee. Therefore the legislation went on the statute books on the definite understanding that it was not insurance, was not intended to be insurance and did not have the effect of giving insurance. I wanted to make that plain at the beginning.
The legislation was then placed on the statute books and we operated under it for some time. I think I should state in a few words what the objective was in bringing it before the house at that time. We had gone through one of the most difficult drought periods ever experienced in western Canada. We had had seven years of continuous drought, two complete crop failures in that seven years and partial crop failures in the other years. This affected a very considerable part of the prairie provinces, a comparatively small part of Manitoba, a very large part of the province of Saskatchewan and a considerable part of the province of Alberta, and during the period preceding the coming into office of a Liberal government in 1935 and as far back as 1931 assistance had been given to that whole area because of the poor crops that had been experienced during that period.
I think it is correct to say that the total assistance given by the federal government, first under Mr. Bennett and later under Mr. King, was not all given to farmers but was given in part to people living in the villages and towns in the area, who were doing business with farmers, and it amounted to approximately $186 million. That, of course, was a very considerable amount of money. In addition, church organizations across Canada, in the eastern part of Canada particularly and even in some sections of western Canada, gathered together food and clothing and distributed it in these areas so that there was quite a considerable amount of money spent and a great deal of work involved in taking care of that area under those circumstances.
But those of us who lived in that section of the country at that time had an idea that there was something much more important, so far as the difficulties were concerned, than the amount of money expended, and that was the effect that living under conditions of that kind had on a great number of people and more particularly on the young people. Having, as has been suggested several times in the house this session, a feeling that it is important to encourage young people born and raised on farms to remain on the farms, we brought in t'nis particular legislation in the hope that in the future it would not be necessary for relief to be sent to that area and

distributed in the way in which it had been and that if there were difficulties in connection with maintaining people in the area, assistance would be rendered by reason of the fact that home builders, heads of families, at least would have some funds with which to pay accounts that had been run for the purpose of maintaining the population through the years when there was drought or when for some other reason crops were destroyed.
Therefore we brought in this legislation and at first it was suggested that the whole cost of a measure of this kind be met from the same source as was the $186 million that had been spent in the preceding years, that is, that it should be taken out of the treasury of Canada and paid as an indication that all Canadians were most desirous of having the population remain in that section of western Canada to produce the very considerable amounts of wealth that come from time to time in the form of cereal grains and livestock of one kind or another.
The legislation was passed and I think it is correct to say it was passed by the house almost unanimously, if not unanimously. I do not remember that any votes were polled against the legislation at any time. There were opinions expressed with regard to details of the legislation and changes that might be made but the legislation had the almost unanimous, if not unanimous, support of the house at that time. The legislation has been on the statute books from then until now and there have been certain results. Before going further, I should say that while the legislation was going through the house a suggestion was made that the cost should not all be met out of the treasury because after all there are quite a number of people in western Canada who do not have crop failures. I happen to be fortunate enough to live in an area where there is very seldom a crop failure. I think we had two during the drought period, one in 1931 and another in 1937, but outside of those two years we have never had a total crop failure, and in the township in which I happen to farm we have never drawn anything under the act since the legislation came into force.
But those who lived in such areas made representations through the farm organizations that it might render the legislation more permanent and result in there being less criticism of it elsewhere if the farmers themselves would agree to make some payment. Therefore it was decided finally to impose a one per cent levy on all grain delivered to the elevators, the amount to be collected at the elevators and turned over to the fund.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act I repeat that the levy was never intended at any time to be a premium paid for insurance, nor was it intended that its payment should give any particular rights to any particular person. As a matter of fact, it was done to emphasize the fact that, while the people of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver were paying through taxes towards the fund, the farmers who lived in the areas desired to pay something in addition to what was taken out of the treasury for the fund in order to make payments possible. The result has been that over the years from the time the fund was first set up down to the present $94,990,566 has been paid into the fund under the one per cent levy. There has been paid out of the same fund $183,576,041. In other words there has been paid out almost twice as much as has been paid in by the farmers. In short, no attempt has been made to make this an insurance plan where premiums are paid for the right to draw from the fund. Of course, as I said a moment ago, there are some areas in which the drought has not been so serious as it has been in other areas. There are some areas, even in the middle of the province of Saskatchewan, that have never drawn out of this fund and there are other areas that have drawn under it in all but two years since the fund was set up. Not everybody in those areas has done so but some people in those areas have drawn in all but two years.
It was natural that some of those in the areas who pay in as much per bushel as any one else pays in but who have drawn out little as compared with what others have drawn, have been raising some criticism with regard to the fund and have been making studies from time to time as to whether or not some better system could be evolved or whether some system of crop insurance might be set up. There have been set up three different commissions, two in Manitoba and one in Saskatchewan, which have studied the question. I have here the report of the second commission set up in Manitoba. That report was made on December 1, 1954. I am going to read only that section of it which deals with prairie farm assistance:
The terms of reference do not empower the commission to make recommendations and none have been made. The commission was directed to consider three questions (set out in the preamble to this report) and to propose answers. As a result of the investigations made and the consideration that has been given to these questions the commission has reached the following conclusions.
I am going to read only the first one because it is the conclusion that refers to prairie farm assistance. The question submitted to the commission was to the effect

Prairie Farm Assistance Act that they wanted to know whether the levy which was made in Manitoba would raise sufficient funds to establish and maintain a crop insurance plan. Their conclusion was this:
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in operation during a period of relatively high average yields; for that reason the record of collections and indemnities on which the Manitoba farmers relied to support their claim that they have been subsidizing Saskatchewan and Alberta farmers, does not present an accurate picture of the operation of the act on a long-term basis.
Next:
If the act had come into operation in 1926 the amount paid to Manitoba farmers in indemnities would now have exceeded the amount produced by the levy by some millions of dollars.
I should say that in the document it is stated that it would be about $13 million.
If the act is continued in force for a long period of time and the present levy of 1 per cent is maintained, all evidence indicates that the indemnities paid will exceed the sum collected by a substantial amount.
In other words, that means that a collection of the one per cent levy would not maintain an insurance plan, even on the basis as set out in prairie farm assistance. Then the report goes on to say this:
If Manitoba did not come under the act and the one per cent levy now paid by Manitoba farmers was maintained, with the intention of using the money collected to reduce the impact of crop hazards, the sum available would be quite inadequate to provide any form of all-risk crop insurance.
Then next:
If, over a period of time, Manitoba farmers received indemnities amounting to more than a dollar for each dollar collected, there can be little doubt that Saskatchewan and Alberta farmers will receive more for each dollar collected than they have received up to this time.
Then last:
The claim made by farmers who appeared before the commission that the method provided in the act for determining which farmers shall be paid is unjust might well receive the consideration of those responsible for the act.
In other words, they suggest that the amount of money which is paid in could not be utilized successfully for the setting up of all-risk crop insurance.

They go into the whole
plan in this report. I do not want to go into it at this stage. I was going to make this suggestion to the committee. I was going to suggest that when this bill is brought in, it be referred to the committee on agriculture and that all these questions such as those that are covered in reports like this might

be brought out during discussion'. I think it would be better to have that done than to try to cover them all here.
But the outcome of this report is to the effect that prairie farm assistance is doing a certain work which it was set up to do but that it could not be made the basis, in so far as collections are concerned, of a crop insurance plan. They think, of course, that if a crop insurance plan could be set up, it would be most helpful to the farmers of Manitoba.
I have here the ninth report of the province of Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life made just last fall and this is the issue on crop insurance. If we are going to have a full discussion on this question, I would recommend to hon. members that they get a copy of this document and read it. It is most helpful because it goes into the whole question of insurance in the United States. It indicates that the crop insurance schemes that are in existence there are set up with $100 million, I think, in support put into the fund by the federal government. Then they have set up a system under which they actually write crop insurance much in the same way as our hail insurance is written in this country -agents go out and write the insurance- after having determined-I think it is clear from this report that this is correct-that there are some areas that could not carry crop insurance because they do not produce endugh to be able to carry crop insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
May I ask the minister this
question? Does the United States system apply to crops other than wheat?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Yes; it does. It is intended to cover and it does cover those kinds of crops grown in those areas. There are in some sections plans that are confined more to wheat and cereal than to the other crops. But generally speaking it is an insurance plan that might cover any crop. But the important feature of it as related to prairie farm assistance is that they feel that they cannot carry on crop insurance with the idea of paying back the money which they obtained from the federal government. They cannot carry it on in areas of low crop production. It can only be carried on in areas of high crop production. It therefore does not attack the problem which prairie farm assistance attacks in this country.
After having gone into all these matters they deal with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act at page 102. After having stated one or two views which they hold they say this:
Recommendation No. 28. That whatever developments take place in crop insurance, P.F.A.A. be

continued in order to assure a minimum level of crop loss protection in all the agricultural areas of the prairie provinces.
That is all I wish to read at the moment. After referring to the two commission reports I just wish to say that they both find that P.F.A.A. serves a purpose, and one which it should continue to serve, and that some consideration ought to be given to whether or not some form of crop insurance can be set up.
Then, too, it is pretty well decided that, constitutionally, crop insurance can only be set up by the provinces. I think it is agreed that, if that be the case, it would be almost impossible to set it up. They say, therefore, that perhaps some experimental plan might be carried on with the idea of determining just what assistance would have to be given.
I only say that in order to suggest to the committee that I think it is important this legislation should remain on the statute books and that it should be dealt with in the light of the experiences we have had with it. One of the experiences which we had with it during those years was that the farmers of the area consisting of Manitoba and extending over the east side of Saskatchewan covering about one third of the province, pay more money into the fund than they get out of it. Then, you have an area which extends across the west side of Saskatchewan, the central part of Saskatchewan and into the province of Alberta, where payments have been high. I think the hon. member for Acadia will agree with me when I say that his constituency covers an area which received the highest payments in the province of Alberta. This high payment area extends from there east across the province of Saskatchewan down to the Soo line in the south and the Regina-Prince Albert line in the central part of the province.
Now, I have examined these figures very carefully, and I have read what the reports say about them. The Manitoba report indicates that, at the time the report was written, out of every dollar the farmers paid in they only got about 62 cents out. I have a later report than that which includes the last two years and this report indicates they received 79 cents out of each dollar. I call your attention to the fact that the last two years cover the period since we amended this act. We amended the act in 1955 and made the amendments apply to the 1954 crop, so payments on the 1954 and 1955 crops are on a different basis from what they were before. The difference is that we brought in the flooded areas and those which, partly because of excessive moisture, were affected by rust. We made payments in the areas on the east side of Saskatchewan and right through Manitoba on a much higher level than had been 82715-91i
Prairie Farm Assistance Act done before. The result was that during those two years there was considerably more taken out of the fund than was paid in.
I have the exact figures here, both for what was paid in and what was taken out. They are contained in a return which was requested by the hon. member for Lisgar. In 1954-55, just using the round figures, there was paid in $748,000 in Manitoba, and in the same year there was paid out in Manitoba, $5,259,000. The next year there was paid in about the same amount, $731,000, and there was paid out $2,150,000, in Manitoba.
Now, in commenting upon what the report says with regard to the relationship of these payments in Saskatchewan and Alberta, I would point out that those figures indicate there was five times as much paid to the farmers in Manitoba in those two years as was paid by them into the fund. They also indicate that there was three and a half times as much paid out in Saskatchewan as was paid in, and in Alberta it was two and a half times. The commission's report indicated that even if you left the levy at 1 per cent and kept the other payments the same as they had been, eventually Manitoba would be getting more out than they paid in. However, the amendments which were made two years ago resulted in considerably more being paid out in the Manitoba area and the eastern part of Saskatchewan than was paid in the earlier years. I think the same thing would apply to the Peace River district of Alberta and the area down between Edmonton and Calgary but in the area through Acadia it would be as I indicated a few minutes ago.
This has been the situation up until now. The proposals made two years ago were to the effect that we had put this act on the statute books in 1939; that at that time farmers were getting 56 cents a bushel for their wheat and later on, in the period we were discussing it, the figure used was about $1.56 or somewhere in that neighbourhood. It was suggested, I think by me as minister at the time, that that possibility was calculated back in 1939, and that as the price of wheat went up there would be less and less necessity for payments in the categories where wheat was delivered for sale. If you get into the category from five bushels up, as it was then, to eight, then there is a possibility that anywhere from three to six bushels to the acre might be sold. Of course, then, the farmer got a better return, along with what was paid out of prairie farm assistance, when he sold that much wheat at the price it was in 1955 as compared with the earlier price.
But there was another argument put up at that time which I realized was a strong argument, namely that when the farmer was down into the lower category, from four

Prairie Farm Assistance Act bushels down, he had a crop failure. Even at four bushels one could not possibly have more than two bushels of wheat to sell and there was very little chance of having that much to sell. It was said then that a man did not get the return from his wheat; his costs were very much higher and his store bills were very much higher than they were before. Even if you were just trying to assist the person to pay his store bills so he could go on living in that area without relief, there should be more paid in the lower categories. It is in connection with that point that we are considering amending the act at the present time, in order to see to it that recognition is given to both of these claims, that is the fact that where you have more wheat to sell there is not as much required by way of assistance and the fact that where you have no wheat to sell considerably more is required in the way of assistance.
In the bill, as I intend to introduce it, provision will be made for an increase in payments. Under section 6 we have tried out two different systems which we have administered by adding to or taking away from the areas. Hon. members who come from that section of the country will know that we have a great block of prairie country which is subject to drought from time to time. In the year 1954, for example, there were more than
150,000	farmers-I will just use the round figures of 150,000-in that area who drew assistance under this plan. I know that whenever anyone goes out to hold meetings across the country there are a great many complaints. However, when you have 150,000 being paid without getting complaints from probably more than a thousand-that may seem quite a lot if you get complaints from a thousand-but it is not quite as big a problem from the point of view of administration as some would make it appear.
But at the same time there is the problem of the areas just on the edge of qualification. Fortunately, probably, Manitoba is very nearly all on the edge and the north-eastern part of Saskatchewan is on the edge. Most of the troubles you have are in the areas where there have not previously been crop failures, but there is a limited number that do complain in areas where there have been failures. The amendments of two years ago took care of that to a certain extent and the amendments which are being brought in now will take care of it to an even greater extent. That being the case I would like to have the resolution passed. I do not think it is necessary to go into any greater detail at this time. I simply wanted to outline what the intention was in the beginning and what the intention still is and I think I might indicate that if we can pass the

resolution in order to base a bill upon it I will be in a position to bring the bill before the committee at an early time. I could not do so today because the bill is not yet in print but I could bring it in within 24 or 48 hours. We could then submit the bill to the committee on agriculture and allow all the details of it to be discussed and bring it back here for further discussion. If this meets with the consent of the committee I should like to proceed in that way. If the committee desires to discuss it at greater length at this time of course I cannot raise any objection to that because that is within the rules of the house and may be done.

Mr. Chairman, as a member coming from western Canada I welcome the announcement of the amendments to this important piece of legislation. In presenting his review the minister suggested that we limit the discussion as much as possible so that we might proceed at the earliest possible moment to consideration of the bill. However, there has been such continuing discussion on this subject of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in my own province of Manitoba that I think I should take a few moments of the committee's time to present some aspects of this legislation which were not emphasized by the minister in his remarks.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to interrupt. I was about to continue my remarks and possibly cover what the hon. member has in mind but I paused to answer some questions which were directed to me and I got away from the subject.
I said that two things had been tried out. In the first place we took the rectangular blocks when we were adding to that big block of townships. It was my intention to amplify my comments when I was distracted by some questions. We operated under rectangular blocks for ten years and under contiguous blocks for four or five years or so. For two years we tried it again on the basis of rectangular blocks and we are now proposing an amendment to the act to put it back on the basis of contiguous blocks. I just wanted to complete my remarks on that subject before the hon. member proceeded.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
I am glad to have that clarification, Mr. Chairman, because I was going to raise that particular point in my remarks. However, I wish to return to a basic problem arising from the remarks the minister has made. It is quite true that this piece of legislation was established in 1939 as a measure to substitute for the program of relief that had been carried out in the prairies during the drought period of the 1930's. I think the fact that the minister has emphasized again today that this is a substitute for a relief measure and not a crop insurance program serves to underline the criticism that arises concerning the P.F.A.A. program in the province of Manitoba. The year 1939 is almost 20 years ago. Actually the legislation placed on the statute books in 1939 came about after the real problem of drought had already disappeared.
The critical years of the dry period were in the mid thirties and by 1939 we were returning to a more normal pattern of moisture in the prairie region. The peak of the problem with which this particular legislation attempts to deal had been passed by the time it arrived on the statute books. This is the reason for the criticism which arises in growing intensity in the province of Manitoba. A great many resolutions have been presented in the provincial legislature, by private members who normally support the party at Ottawa, severely criticizing the P.F.A.A.
I maintain that in re-emphasizing the relief aspects of the legislation the minister fails completely to take into consideration the tremendous changes that have taken place in our agricultural economy generally since 1939. These changes have been referred to in the house time and time again from this

Prairie Farm Assistance Act side of the chamber. I have made reference to them many times myself. They have placed an entirely different complexion upon our agricultural economy.
In western Canada today we do not need a relief measure, we need something which will provide strong underlying income stability. The minister pointed out that during the thirties relief payments became necessary so that the farm housewife could meet her grocery bills. That is just one part of the cash problem facing the prairie farmer today. His whole activity has become deeply involved financially. He is now operating on a cash basis rather than under a subsistence economy. He needs cash for much more than the paying of grocery bills or even to meet the first call on his income, his municipal taxes. He needs a stable cash income in order to carry on the process of farming. Most of our farms are mechanized. Formerly the farmer could produce his fuel in the form of feed and fodder for his horses, but today he cannot move unless he has the necessary cash wherewithal to keep his machinery rolling and to pay for the gas and other things required in the mechanized process of farming.
While we welcome the amendments to the act which have been outlined by the Minister of Agriculture, while these amendments are improvements, they are simply stop-gap measures until such time as we can deal with the whole problem of income stability and cash stability in our prairie economy. Increased payments to the farmer under the P.F.A.A. are at least a step in the right direction.
The suggestions and comments offered from time to time by members of the opposition, and even by government members from western Canada, concerning the fundamental changes taking place in our prairie agricultural economy, have been recently reinforced by the independent viewpoint of the members of the Gordon commission. We have farmers moving away from the farm and we have farms becoming larger. This trend is going to continue for the next 25 years. Certainly a measure devised in 1939 to deal with a problem which existed in the mid thirties is not adequate to deal with the problem of agricultural stability in 1957.
Manitoba has been especially interested in the shortcomings of this legislation because that province has been particularly affected. In his survey the minister pointed out that it is doubtful if Manitoba will ever receive compensation equal to what has been contributed in the form of the universal levy because that province is not affected to such a great extent as Saskatchewan or Alberta
[Mr. Dlnsdale.l

by marginal land. This is one point upon which the farmers of Manitoba continually harp. If that situation is to continue it means continuing discrimination against one province.
As the minister pointed out, several attempts have been made in the Manitoba legislature to devise a crop insurance program that would serve more efficiently and effectively the particular needs of Manitoba. The committee of 1955 is the most recent attempt of this kind. While it did not make any specific recommendations concerning the possibility of introducing a crop insurance plan in Manitoba it certainly indicated that such a program was greatly to be desired.
Not only is there general discrimination against the province of Manitoba in the operation of this act, there is discrimination on an individual basis too. This causes the greatest protest on the part of the individual farmer. It is only infrequently that large areas of Manitoba become qualified for benefits under the act and invariably when that has happened in my constituency there has been a storm of protest from the farmers in the areas affected. During the time these farmers were contributing their 1 per cent levy they were under the impression that should they suffer a crop failure as a result of one of the numerous acts of nature to which the agricultural economy is subject they would be adequately covered by P.F.A.A. Almost without exception they become sadly disillusioned when the actual payments are made. They find that under the block system of payments there is discrimination as between neighbours. You are either "in" or you are "out" and if you are "out", and just across the fence from the block area there is, of course, a very strong feeling of injustice which arises when you see your neighbour, who might not have been so severely affected as yourself, receiving the benefits of the P.F.A. payments while you do not, even though you might have suffered an almost 100 per cent crop loss.
This situation was again brought forcibly to my attention last summer, and fall. We had a very severe hail storm which swept right over the heart of my constituency and the damage resulting from the storm amounted to some $20 million. I was called to attend protest meetings all over the area. Once the P.F.A. payments were forthcoming it was suddenly realized that this legislation was totally inadequate to meet the problem, raised by this particular kind of damage.
Incidentally, with regard to that point, I received from the municipality of Oakland an excellent presentation with regard to this particular matter. This submission has, I think, already been received by the Minister

of Agriculture, so he will be aware of its contents. It has been very carefully drawn up. I do not want to take up the time of the committee by reading the recommendations it contains. I do not know whether or not it would be possible to get them on the record. The document does, Mr. Chairman, make some specific recommendations for suitable amendments, and as I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by reading it into the record I am wondering if, perhaps, I could have permission to put it on Hansard for today. It is a carefully prepared document and hon. members might like to have the opportunity of seeing it.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act have repeatedly been made concerning the inadequacies of prairie farm assistance legislation. A particular difficulty which has arisen in recent days in my area-and I think this is a general condition throughout western Canada-from the cost-price squeeze to which agriculture has been subjected as the result of the very drastic changes which are taking place in the Canadian economy, is that a good many of our farmers have found it necessary, in order to maintain solvency of their farms, to take up temporary employment off the farm. The minister makes the point that as far as crop insurance is concerned only the provincial governments can take the necessary legislative action. Prairie Farm Assistance Act any action in this regard would require initiative on the part of the federal government.
It is a case of "passing the buck" between the two levels of government-something which happens far too frequently for the good of our farmers in Canada today. But despite what is contained in the commission's report and despite what the minister has said the fact still remains that from the time the legislation went into effect in 1939 up to the present the picture in Manitoba has been that the farmers have paid through the one per cent levy a great deal more money than they have taken out of the fund. I do not know the exact figures, but I understand we will have them on the record later. In any event, it is my information that up to the present time Manitoba farmers have received approximately 64 cents out of every dollar they have paid into the fund.
In these circumstances it is to be expected that there will be a considerable number of complaints and discontent with respect to the operation of the legislation. But I want to say quite clearly that I take the same attitude with respect to the act on this occasion as I have taken consistently since entering the house, that until something better comes along, until we get a system like crop insurance that will operate on an individual basis I am one of those who advocate that no province should withdraw from the operations of the act, if that were possible. With all its faults and weaknesses, I believe that the act is the only thing available at the present time which provides some compensation in case of a serious crop failure in our province, and in my opinion it would not be wise at this time to get rid of the modest coverage we do have and have nothing in its place. Therefore my efforts and those, I believe, of most members from Manitoba, will be directed towards the improvement of the act at every opportunity until something better comes along.
Some of the difficulties in qualifying were described by the member for Brandon-Souris, but there are one or two other points that should be mentioned. One difficulty arises from the fact that the qualifying clause in the act or the yardstick which decides who qualifies and who does not is based on the production of wheat. In many parts of our province wheat is not the chief crop and it is

quite possible that if another crop were used for the yardstick, barley, for example, the results would be quite different from the results obtained by using wheat. That is one reason we often find areas which ordinarily could be considered crop failure areas in the sense that there is sometimes a total crop failure of barley or oats but where there happen to be a few patches of wheat here and there in the township which bring the average over 8 bushels per acre, thus automatically ruling out the whole area as far as prairie farm assistance is concerned.
There is another matter I should like to put forward for the minister's consideration. Perhaps sooner or later, if the trend in Manitoba continues with respect to the amounts paid in and the amounts paid out of the fund and the farmers of Manitoba continue to pay in more than they receive from the fund, the time will come when the minister will have to consider a zoning system because the cost of production and the yield experience is not the same throughout the three prairie provinces. In other words, it costs more to maintain the land in some parts of the prairie provinces and of course the average yield is greater. In other parts it costs less to maintain the land and the average yield is lower. Therefore it is not always possible to put them all in the same category and achieve fairness. I think the time may be coming when, as the result of experience, we may have to work out a zoning system whereby in those areas where, generally speaking, the cost of production and average yield are higher over a period of years the qualifying yield will also be higher whereas in those areas where the cost of production and the average yield are generally lower the qualifying yield will also be lower. That would be one way of bringing about greater fairness in the payment of compensation under the act.
I think that the idea of crop insurance should not be abandoned altogether. The minister has set out some of the difficulties and he maintains that if there is to be crop insurance then it is a provincial responsibility under our constitution. Even if that is so, I do not think there is anything to prevent the federal government from taking a hand with respect to crop insurance by underwriting the provinces should they be able to set up some sort of plan amongst themselves. I think the minister will agree, after having read the reports of the committees and commissions that have studied crop insurance in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, that none of these committees or commissions has recommended at any time against crop insurance as such.
But they came to the conclusion that crop insurance on a premium basis would not be able to sustain itself. The time may come
Prairie Farm Assistance Act when the prairie provinces, or for that matter any number of provinces, may wish to evolve a crop insurance plan and to ask the federal government to underwrite that plan at least for a period of years in order to take care of any unusual or disastrous experience. In those circumstances if the federal government were willing to act as the underwriter for a crop insurance plan which is set up on a provincial basis or co-operatively among a group of provinces, I think it may have some chance of success.
The minister has given us a rough idea of what the increases are to be in the various categories in the awards under this act. Although they do not go as far as does the resolution which I have on the order paper,
I am glad to support the resolution because it is an improvement over what we now have. The minister expressed some doubt as to what may be done about the levy. It is at that point particularly that I want to bring to his attention this argument. In effect since the act came into force in 1939 the levy has been increasing, although in the act it is still one per cent. But if it was one per cent of the price of a bushel of wheat in 1939, which price at that time was somewhere about 70 cents, the price of wheat is now more than double that and the levy is still one per cent of the price. In effect, the amount that the farmer is paying into the fund has just about doubled since 1939. Although the percentage figure is still the same, the amount per bushel that he is paying on his grain under this levy has just about doubled. So all during that period of years, when the effective amount that he was paying per bushel has been increased along with the price of the grain, the awards under the act remained the same. There was no increase in them. Now that we have finally come around to providing for an increase in the awards, I think that if we were to maintain even the same position as that which obtained in 1939, in effect the farmers have already paid the extra levy for this increase. I would strongly recommend at this time that the levy be not increased, particularly with respect to the farmers in Manitoba.
As I have already said, there has been a great deal of discontent and criticism and, as time passes, there probably will be more. But if at the same time, as the figures show, the Manitoba farmers are drawing only about 64 cents for every dollar they put in and if [DOT] they are asked to put more in, I am afraid it will not be a very popular move in my province. I therefore hope that the minister and the government will come to the conclusion that at least for a period of years, as a trial period, we carry on with the one per

I am glad to hear that it
is the intention to leave it at one per cent. It will be good news in Manitoba, I can assure the minister.
I was about to point out that the chances of crop failure, unless we consider something extremely unusual, iri my opinion are on the decline. The production per farm and the production per man on the farm have been increasing in western Canada. With new methods of farming new fertilizer, new types of machinery and so on, I think that the farmers themselves are doing a great deal to minimize the danger of crop failure. Of course there are some circumstances which are completely beyond the control of any farmer such as a severe drought, a severe flood, an early frost or things of that kind. But ordinarily speaking-and I think the report of the Gordon commission bears this out-farming methods and the approach of the farmer to technological methods are working towards greater stability of production in western Canada and towards minimizing the chances of crop failure. If that trend continues it should mean that there will be less and less call upon this fund under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act from time to time. I am therefore fairly sure that it would be wiser to leave the levy as it is at the present time and try out the increases in the awards.
These increases are sorely needed. Of course I should like to have seen them greater than they are. According to the latest statistics, even last year, in 1956, the cost of production on the farm increased by 6.5 per cent. That trend has been going on for a number of years. The cost of production has been coming up year after year since about 1946. That means that when there is a crop failure the farmer stands to lose to a much greater extent today than was the case ten years ago because he has invested, in terms of operating expenses, more in the attempt to produce than was the case previously.
Having made those general comments I wish to express my support for the resolution and my appreciation of the fact that the government has decided to leave the levy as it is. However, I want to raise one more question. In doing so I want to make it clear that I am not raising this question because of any undue suspicion in my own mind but rather because there have come to my attention-as I am 
COMMONS	.
sure have come to the attention of many hon. members from the prairies-accusations and charges of political interference in the administration of this act. I want to make it quite clear'

and I emphasize this point-that I am one of those who have never in this house or outside of it charged with or accused the government or those who administer this act of political interference. But because an increasing number of farmers are writing to me and in conversations are telling me that they are becoming convinced that there is political interference, I feel that it is my duty at this time to bring the matter to the attention of the minister and of the committee. If there is anything that will destroy the effectiveness of an act of this kind, it is a conviction on the part of the farmers that it is being used for political purposes. It is my hope that the minister, sometime during this discussion, will make a categorical statement before this committee in order to assure it and to assure the country and the farmers

because, after all, it is to a large extent their money that is involved-that this act is being administered impartially and fairly and is not being used under any circumstances for political purposes.
Particularly in the province of Manitoba the implication is rather serious because, as I have already pointed out, the farmers in Manitoba have paid into that fund a considerable amount of money more than they have taken out of it over the period from 1939 to 1956. If they become convinced that their own money-and may I again emphasize the fact that it is their own money; there has not been one cent of government money going to the farmers of Manitoba over this period- that is coming back to them in the form of prairie farm assistance is being used in this way, and if somebody is attempting to play politics with their own money-in other words to try to bribe them with their own money to vote in a certain way-then that is adding insult to injury.
I also want to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that it is my belief that the suspicions and distrust with regard to the administration of this act and the charges of political interference arise out of the activities of the Liberal candidates, ex-candidates or ex-members as the case may be in my province.
As I have said, I have not at any time- nor do I know of any other member from our province who has done so-charged political interference. But there have been Liberal candidates who have gone around and apparently have successfully persuaded a number of farmers that they are in a position to interfere politically in order to bring benefits to certain farmers as a return for their political support.

Xu should not be my function here to defend the Liberal candidates in my province, or to defend the government against charges of political interference. I do this because I think it should be made clear that this act, which is being financed partly by the farmers themselves and partly out of the public treasury, should be kept free from political interference that might destroy its effectiveness.
I hope the minister will make a statement to the effect that so far as his department is concerned there is no political interference that he knows of, and that no attempt has ever been made to use the act for purposes of political partisanship. If he does not do so, then more and more farmers are going to be persuaded that the Liberal candidates who are running around the country claiming to be the distributors of the largesse under this act are right. If that conviction gains ground in Manitoba he is going to have a minor revolution on his hands. This is said as a suggestion for the minister's own benefit and for the benefit of the administration of this act. I hope he will make that statement, because I think it is long overdue. I shall reserve any further comments I have to make until the bill is before us.

In this particular bill the evidence was heard by a subcommittee of the other place. The age of the applicant Leonard Bloom, is 30, and that I submit is a rather young age for a man to be petitioning the parliament of Canada for release from his marriage vows. He was asked when he was married

and he replied on December 14, 1950. At one point he claimed that he lived with his wife until 1951 but he later amended that to February, 1952.
Mr. Speaker, from December 14, 1950 to February 1952 is barely 15 months. Certainly this young man did not give his marriage much of a chance to succeed, when after such a relatively short period of time he decided he could no longer tolerate being married to his wife.
The evidence indicated that his wife left him in February, 1952. He then produced a photograph of his wife and was asked the following questions as reported at page 8 of the evidence:
Q. Is it a good likeness of your wife?
A. It is.
Q. Do you remember when it was taken?
A. I couldn't say offhand.

It seems very odd indeed that a woman who left her husband in 1952 would supply him with a photograph of herself for use on January 22, 1957. You told us you lived together with your wife until February 1952. Will you tell us what happened in February 1952?
The only answer the applicant was able to give was:
Well, she left, saying that she was going on a holiday and she told me where she was going. I phoned her up where she was supposed to go and she had not arrived there.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, before I make my remarks in connection with this bill, I want to assure the hon. member for Portneuf that I do not love to talk about these things, but that I recognize my responsibility and that, unlike him, when a vote is called I am here for that vote. This bill deals with the petition-

speechtext: Order. In what he has just said the hon. member is perhaps forgetting that an hon. member is not obliged to vote when a vote is called. Therefore for one hon. member who has chosen to vote on a certain division to say that another member is not fulfilling his responsibility because he has not chosen to vote is, in my opinion, to misconstrue the duty of a member. Mr. Speaker, I accept your correction. I wish only to point out that I do not believe you were in the chair when some rather unkind remarks were made about me and my rights by the hon. member for Portneuf. I realize full well that he may believe quite honestly that he has met his obligation by not voting on the amendment that was before us. I quite appreciate

Private Bills-Divorce
the fact that we all have the privilege of refraining from voting. However, I find it a little bit difficult to note that the rest of us, or at least some of us, are obligated to deal with these matters when they appear on the order paper. The whole contention of our argument is that we believe these things should be removed from the order paper.
This particular case deals with the petition of Frances May Cousins Stone for a divorce from Harry Walter Stone. The case is unique in that the petitioner herself does not appear. She is apparently a resident elsewhere. In the evidence as we have it, as taken on January 22, 1957, before the subcommittee of the other house, the chairman explains this when he states as follows:
We are proceeding with this case, Mr. Gaboury, and I understand that we are to hear two witnesses. We may require you to give further evidence with regard to this woman who is living in British Columbia and says that she cannot come to attend this hearing, because I was not satisfied with the affidavit you submitted. It is only because these witnesses are here at considerable expense, and that some confusion has arisen, that we are taking this unusual course. It is not a precedent at all that we are hearing this case without the applicant being present.
Then Mr. Gaboury says this:
I have a Mrs. McCall, whom I wish to call. I subpoenaed the respondent, and I know he is here Perhaps he may be called?
The petitioner is then called but does not appear. The respondent is called, appears and remains in the room. Mr. Gaboury then says:
Mrs. McCall is my only witness, Mr. Chairman, unless the respondent wants to testify; I do not know yet.
So here, Mr. Speaker, we have a divorce being recommended with the petitioner absent, a most unusual case. Instead of the customary several independent witnesses, we have only one witness and the husband who may also testify. Who is this witness? I quote from the report:
Q. What is your full name?
A. Blanche McCall.
Q. What is your age?
A. Seventy.
Q. Where do you live?
ft- Seventy-two Oxford street, Guelph, Ontario.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Housewife.
Here is another oddity in that the petitioner lives in British Columbia, as I have said before, and the only independent witness lives in Guelph, in the province of Ontario. She is then shown a photograph which has been annexed to the petition of the petitioner and she is asked to identify it:
Q. Do you see him here today?
A. Yes, I see him.
Q. That is Mr. Stone here?
A. Yes.

Q. I beg your pardon, what is his name?
A. Harry Stone.
Q. Do you know him as Harry Stone?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you had occasion to meet him anywhere else before today?
A. Yes, he was living at a room in my home.
Q. That was where?
A. In Guelph, Ontario.
Q. How long did he live there with you?
A. He came in May, 1955 and lived until, I think, the middle of March 1956.
Her acquaintance therefore, with this man, is limited to the province of Ontario. Then she is asked if he came there alone, and I quote:
Q. How did he go there alone, was he alone as a tenant of yours or was he accompanied by anyone?
A. He came alone, he told me that his wife was living in Toronto and expected to be confined in six weeks time, and after that six weeks expired he brought a woman I call Mrs. Stone to the house.
Q. Now, this woman that he designated as Mrs. Stone-I hereby show you a photograph which has been annexed to the petitioner's affidavit as exhibit B; would that be the lady who accompanied him?
A. No.
Q. There is no doubt in your mind that it is not the lady?
A. No.
Q. How did they live there at your place during that period from May 1955 until March 1956?
A. She came six weeks after he came there; they occupied the same room.
The witness then says there was only one bed in the room and they occupied the same room. He had referred to her as his wife. The witness did not know, I presume, that this was not the man's wife. However, she does know that the woman who lived with him as Mrs. Stone is not the same woman as the woman whose picture she is being shown by Mr. Gaboury, the attorney.
The chairman of the committee investigates a bit further by asking:
Q. Was Mr. Stone there when she told you that?
He is referring to the fact she was expecting a baby.
A. Mr. Stone brought her to my house.
Q. That is true, but you are telling of a conversation now and I want to know whether Mr. Stone was present when she made the statement that you are now going to tell us about?
A. As near as I can remember I was surprised when they came and he did not have the baby and I asked what about the baby?
Q. They were both there at the time?
A. They were both there at the time, and Mrs. Stone said because Harry had never worked too much the children's aid society were taking the baby to look after it.
This all happened in the province of Ontario. I am not sure how this petition comes to us here, except that the lady is no longer living with him, and I imagine he is now living in a province whose rules make it compulsory for her to go to live there to obtain a divorce or else come to this parliament in order to be granted relief.

Then the chairman very carefully points out to Mr. Stone, before he testifies, the position of affairs with regard to him:
You are here present and therefore you are interested. You are not under any obligation at all to give evidence which might tend to prove your own adultery though you are privileged to do so if you want to do so. If you wish to do so you can go into the witness box and you can answer any questions you like or you can make a statement to us if you wish to do so, and if you do not wish to do so you do not need to. You just make your own choice.
Then Mr. Stone takes the witness stand and admits that he is living in Guelph temporarily. Of course no one knows how long "temporarily" may be in actual fact. If we endorse the principle of this case then we are also automatically saying to people in all parts of Canada that they have a right to petition this parliament for relief from their marriage vows. I think it is as simple as that.
I should like to pose to the house the problem that would arise if this became known throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Apparently this man is not satisfied with the divorce arrangements obtaining in the province of Ontario or, rather, I should say the woman is not satisfied with the arrangements obtaining in the province of Ontario, where I believe she might have to go if she wishes to win a divorce from him. At any rate, she would have to take action in either the courts of British Columbia or the courts of Ontario. He lived in Montreal before that, and says he lived there all his life. The previous witness said he had lived at her home in Guelph for some time, about a year and a half. Logically, I do not think anyone can say he is living there temporarily. I believe it may well be the case that people are finding out how relatively easy it is to get their petition for relief through this house. They are choosing this avenue rather than the proper court procedures that are set up for people in British Columbia and Ontario.
May I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the hour for private bills the Minister of Agriculture got me sidetracked on to the question of hail suppression, but I will now come back to the general operation of the act.
Certainly there are areas in western Canada that have consistently received more under the act than they have paid out, and it is equally true there are areas that have received less than they have paid out. Therefore the attitude of farmers to the resolution before us is bound to be affected at least in part by the area in which they live. The greater part of the Acadia constituency, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture, has been a heavy beneficiary under the act, and naturally they will be in support of the resolution that is before us. They will argue, and I think rightly so, that in view of the fact that costs have more than doubled since the act was first passed, payments should also be substantially increased.
In view of the fact that heavy payments have been made in the Acadia constituency we have heard it argued that these lands should be taken out of production. People have said that the area is too dry. Others have said that the land in that area is submarginal and therefore should be taken out of production.
That may have been true many years ago, but about 27 years ago that whole area was reorganized. Most of the land was sold for tax arrears and taken over as special areas, and then leased back to the farmers in units sufficiently large for them to make a fair living; but they have not been allowed to cultivate submarginal land. We find today that the majority of the land that is farmed in the special areas is good land.
During the past six or seven years that area has had more than normal rainfall; consequently the crops have been quite good. But if we are to judge by the record of the past there is every reason to believe that the area will become dry again. If it does become dry again then there is no doubt that heavy payments will once again be made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
I was quite interested in a statement made by the Gordon commission on this point. I shall read it, because I want to stress the fact that what is said in the report does not apply to the Acadia constituency and I shall explain why. If we turn to page 27 of the preliminary report of the Gordon commission we find these words:
Assistance has been provided also under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to farmers who live in areas where crop failures have occurred from time

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
to time. This also has been a useful program. However, there might be merit in imposing some limit upon the number of years in which payments could be made under this act to people who persist in farming lands which have a high record of crop failures over a term of years. If this were done, assistance should be offered to those people who might be willing to re-establish themselves elsewhere.
As I say, that does not apply to the Acadia constituency for the simple reason that such reorganization has already taken place. Sixty per cent of the farmers who used to live there have moved out. The submarginal land is no longer cultivated. When they talk about assistance being given to move farmers, I would point out that in Acadia assistance is not needed for the purpose of moving farmers out but is needed in the form of irrigation in that area.
For many years there has been discussion about the Red Deer diversion irrigation project. The original survey was made in 1922 and was known as the William Pearson project. Under this project half a million acres of land would be irrigated. The idea would be to provide feed lots to the people farming in that area so they would have sufficient feed to carry their stocks over the winter. If dry years come back, what will happen is that farmers will have to cut down their herds, because they will not be able to raise enough feed to carry their stocks through the winter; and if they do that they will no longer be self-supporting.
For this reason I hope the federal government will be able to work out an agreement with the provincial government under which irrigation can be undertaken in that area. If that is done I am satisfied that this will be one of the most prosperous districts to be found in western Canada. As I say, the land is good and the only thing we are short of is rain. That is the picture in an area where more is received under the act than is paid in levies.
Let us now take the other side of the picture. In the western part of the constituency-and I would say from the constituency northwest-we find the opposite to be the truth. Farmers pay out far more in levies than they receive back in the form of compensation. It is very seldom that those farmers receive any benefit under the act. A farmer can pay to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act fund hundreds of dollars, as they have done; yet if they lose the total crop through hail there is very little chance of their receiving any benefit, the reason being of course that the hail comes in an irregular shape. They cannot qualify because you have to have at least half a township with a yield of less than eight bushels per acre before any benefits can be paid out. The


farmers say they would not mind paying the levy under the act, and they would not mind having the levy increased, if it were guaranteed that in the event of a loss they would receive some form of compensation. In other words they want it to be either on an individual basis or to have a scheme of crop insurance.
In 1955 I spoke at some length in this house on the question of crop insurance, and especially with regard to the operation of crop insurance in the United States. It seems to me that the time is long overdue for a national scheme of all-risk crop insurance in this country. I am not suggesting that this act should be made into a crop insurance scheme. The Minister of Agriculture points out that if we tried to make the Prairie Farm Assistance Act into a crop insurance scheme it would be unconstitutional, and he has suggested that if the provinces want crop insurance the best way would be for a province to put it in.
If there is one thing the federal crop insurance corporation made clear in its report it is this. If you want crop insurance to be successful you have to have it on the widest possible basis. There is very little chance of it succeeding on less than a national basis, and I do not think there would be any chance of it succeeding on a provincial basis. As a matter of fact when Mr. R. E. Motherwell made his report entitled "A Study of Crop Insurance" in 1944 he made this quite clear. On page 35 of the report it is stated:
Since the three prairie provinces are so closely associated in agricultural production, any attempt at crop Insurance could best be handled by federal administration affecting the area now affected by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Admittedly, insurance is not a federal matter but this problem clearly seems one requiring a broader scope than just one province.
I think the experience in the United States fully justifies Mr. Motherwell's statement.
While it might be unconstitutional to turn the Prairie Farm Assistance Act into a crop insurance scheme, I submit there would be nothing unconstitutional about putting in effect a voluntary scheme of crop insurance right across Canada. There are very strong reasons why it should be done on a national basis. In this house we hear continually from eastern Canada and the maritimes to the effect that we are always doing things for western Canada, and no doubt the people in those parts of Canada feel the same way about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. If we could bring in a national crop insurance scheme that would operate from the maritimes to British Columbia, that criticism would no longer be made. Judging by what has happened in the United States there would be a far better chance of a crop

insurance scheme succeeding on that basis than there would if we put it in merely in one province, or even in western Canada.
In the United States crop insurance covers all crops like tobacco, cotton, corn and grain, and there is no reason why we could not have an all-embracing crop insurance scheme to cover all provinces both east and west. If it was decided to have a crop insurance scheme the country could be zoned into districts, where the coverage and premium would be adjusted on the basis of crop conditions which had existed over a period of time. Probably it would be necessary to leave out certain areas where crop failures were occurring continuously. If you tried to put a crop insurance scheme into effect in areas where the risk was high the rates would have to be prohibitive. Such areas could continue to be protected under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In the United States similar areas are covered by a form of relief legislation.
A vote could be taken in each zone to decide whether or not the farmers wanted to continue under the P.F.A.A. or would prefer to come under a crop insurance scheme. Where crop insurance was instituted the Prairie Farm Assistance Act could be discontinued and the levy no longer collected. Any losses to be paid under the P.F.A.A. could be met by the levy in the areas where that act was continued in force, and from the consolidated revenue fund.
I know some hon. members and some people will argue that crop insurance is not feasible, but I think instead of trying to discuss this question on a theoretical basis it would be far better to discuss it in the light of actual experience. The experience of the federal crop insurance corporation of the United States is available to us. Crop insurance has been in operation in the United States since 1938. There was no private crop insurance written in those days except hail insurance. When the act first came into operation the only crop insured was wheat, and then it was extended to cover cotton, flax, tobacco, corn and practically every major crop.
Under that act insurance was written up to 50 per cent or 75 per cent of the average long-term yield. Contracts for one year were signed, requiring renewal each year. Loss adjustments were originally in the hands of local committees. During the first four years of the operation of that act there were heavy losses; from 1938 to 1942 the corporation lost $71 million, $7 million on wheat alone.
The act was suspended in 1944 and it is interesting to note that the report written
Prairie Farm Assistance Act by Mr. Motherwell on federal crop insurance in the United States was based upon the experience of those years. After 1944 the crop insurance act was thoroughly overhauled and a number of adjustments made, and after that it operated successfully.
The changes that were made and which are still applicable were, first, that insurance could be written only up to 75 per cent of the average yield over a long period of time or the actual cash investment in the crop, whichever was the lesser. The coverage and premium rates were to be set by areas instead of on an individual basis as formerly, but adjustment of losses was to be made on an individual basis. Local agents were appointed instead of having local committees, and losses were reported directly to the state director instead of to a local authority.
Largely as a result of these changes there was a considerable improvement in the operation of the act and from 1948 to 1954 the premiums and indemnities were practically in balance, whereas before that there had been heavy losses. It is interesting to remember that from 1948 to 1954 there were some very heavy crop failures in the United States but, as I say, the act weathered the storm and the premiums pretty well balanced the indemnities.
The cost of crop insurance in the United States has been considerably less than the cost of hail insurance in the west. The crop insurance in the United States is all-risk insurance. I think a fair comparison could be made between crop losses in the United States and those in Canada, though probably they do not have the degree of frost we have. On the other hand they have far greater losses in the dust bowl. On the whole I think it is a fair comparison to make.
We find that in the United States the cost of insurance to cover all crops worked out at 6.2 per cent of the protection, and the amount needed to cover the actual loss was 6.7 per cent. Taking wheat alone, the cost was 8.5 per cent of protection and the amount needed to meet the loss was 8.7 per cent. In both cases the premiums kept slightly below the actual cost. I think the report shows quite clearly that all-risk crop insurance can be provided at a reasonable cost so long as you exclude the heavy risk areas. In the United States those areas are kept under certain relief legislation, and in Canada they could be retained under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
I am convinced that in western Canada we should have crop insurance, and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act could be supplementary to that scheme. I do hope the minister will try to get the provinces to

I should like to see the federal government give leadership by passing a federal crop insurance act, and then telling the provinces that any province that agreed to pass enabling legislation would be able to obtain the benefits of the act. I am satisfied that if that were done a majority of the provinces would come in.
