Mr. Chairman, I am not going to enter into a long discussion of the merits of this act. I think all Canada realizes that it is a splendid act and has served a very useful purpose. I hope the minister will see to it that the scope of the act is enlarged in the near future.
I would suggest to him that the time has arrived when the benefits of the act should be applied to the fruit and vegetable growers of Canada as well. I know the plight of some of the growers. If they had been able to take advantage of this act they would have been materially helped. Let me point out that here is a group of farmers in Canada who are just as worthy of assistance as the prairie wheat farmers, and who should be given assistance in the same way.
Perhaps the minister has already given this question some thought, but I would again draw to his attention the serious losses which have been incurred by these people over the last few years and in respect of which no assistance has so far been received from the federal government. I seriously think this act should be made an all-Canadian act, one which would be fair to all producers and growers, which would reach out and cover all farmers and, in particular, those of my own district, who need the services this measure provides to rescue them from the depression which now confronts them.
I earnestly ask the minister to give this question his consideration. I know it cannot be done at this time, and I know, also, that he is fully aware of the bad situation which now exists, particularly in my riding. But I do ask him to give consideration to enlarging the scope of the act to extend it more liberally to all the farmers in Canada, and not to confine it to one preferred group. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been a good deal of discussion today on the question of crop insurance, and as many hon. members have pointed out, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is not, generally speaking, considered to be a crop insurance act in the ordinary sense of the word. However, the act that is presently in force, even with the amendments proposed by the minister, will not be adequate to meet the very high cost of farming at the present time. I believe a good case can be made out for a crop insurance plan that would apply to specialized crop areas in this country. I agree with those who have said that the time has arrived when the government should consider legislation to help fruit producers, tobacco growers and other farmers engaged in the production of specialized crops whenever they experience crop failure.
The United States has had a great deal of experience with regard to crop insurance, and I believe there is much we could gain from a study of that experience. In order to provide a crop insurance scheme the United States first of all set up a crown corporation. The history of this country shows that private enterprise finds it impossible to engage in crop insurance, the main reason being that agricultural producers are unable to pay the very high premiums that would be necessary to make such projects actuarially sound and provide profits from such an undertaking. Nevertheless, I feel that the benefits which would flow from such an act should influence the government to provide a crop insurance scheme.
The minister said this afternoon that when he had the bill before a Senate committee- I believe he said it was in 1939-Senator Arthur Meighen expressed certain opinions as to the legality or otherwise of crop insurance if such a measure were enacted by the federal government. I sent for the minutes of that committee meeting because I was interested in finding out what the senator had said as to the constitutionality of the

matter, but the word I got back from the parliamentary library was that there were no minutes of that committee.
So the minister is relying on his memory as to what Senator Arthur Meighen said. I have read the reports made in connection with crop insurance by R. E. Motherwell and by the Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life, and I have not seen any suggestion that the constitution stands in the way of the federal government embarking on a system of crop insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext: May I call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that this question was discussed in the Quebec legislature within, I think, the last month, and the opinion was expressed very definitely there that cases had been decided on the question.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
In spite of any comments the minister may make at this time I am not convinced that crop insurance schemes are not perfectly within the jurisdiction of the federal government if it should wish to undertake such a program. With regard to many other things the government has done in the past we have heard the same old excuse used many times, the excuse that, after all, certain matters were the responsibility of the provincial governments, and the federal government could not undertake them. We have heard this excuse given in the past with regard to unemployment insurance, with regard to old age pensions, with regard to family allowances, with regard to the Canada Council, with regard to federal aid to university education, and so on. Every year the list grows longer of things the government has said in the past to be unconstitutional but which at some later stage the government has found to be constitutional.
Only last year, in this connection, we were given an opinion by a deputy minister that it was within federal competence to legislate on and control the interest rates and charges made by companies carrying on instalment credit business. The same thing will apply to this question of crop insurance. In the past the government has always said that it was not within federal competence to enact such measures. However, I believe that if the minister and his colleagues wished to set up a system of crop insurance the chances are that they would be able to find eminent constitutional authorities, probably within the government's own service, who would furnish written opinions that such a program was, in fact, constitutional.
Certainly I can see no reason why a federal crown corporation could not engage in crop insurance if the government provided for
Prairie Farm Assistance Act such a corporation to be set up and, in addition, as the hon. member for Acadia has suggested, provided some federal money to enable such a corporation to undertake what is, in fact, a very risky business.
In this connection, the Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life, to which the minister applied the term "an excellent report" this afternoon, states on page 20 that the minister himself, back in 1939, suggested that within the Prairie Farm Assistance Act there was a very definite measure of insurance. They report him, from page 20 of Hansard, as follows:
They say that in the whole history of the organizations they have been advocating crop insurance and have insisted at all times that the farmer himself should make some payment toward it. I believe it would be a mistake to do away with this feature of the legislation. It establishes one of the main features of what will be in the future an insurance plan.
So the minister, I take it from that quotation made in 1939, was stating it as his opinion that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would, in the years ahead, develop an insurance feature and would in fact become an insurance plan.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Yes. The Saskatchewan royal commission points out that there is no experience in this field and no sufficiently detailed records in this country to decide whether or not a crop insurance scheme would in fact be practical. They point out that in some of the very high risk areas the chances are that the premium would be so high that a crop insurance plan would never in fact be practical. They do say there are large areas of western Canada where in all probability crop insurance can be made a practical thing. I imagine that large areas of the province of Manitoba and the whole northeastern section of Saskatchewan would constitute areas in which a crop insurance plan might in fact be operative on a paying basis.
The main recommendation of the Saskatchewan royal commission is that a crop insurance experiment should be conducted within a limited area, and they say the people who should be involved in such an experiment are the federal government. Recommendation No. 1 on page 99 of their report reads as follows:
That an experimental crop insurance program be launched in Saskatchewan as a program complementary to, but separate from, the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act program; and that an intensive effort be made to find means to extend the experimental program to representative areas in the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
If the minister were to follow the recommendation of the Saskatchewan royal commission in this regard, a federal crown corporation would perhaps be set up as the best administrative body to set aside certain areas in western Canada within which crop insurance would be undertaken. The royal commission is very strongly of the opinion that such an experiment should be conducted in a limited way in order to gain firsthand information with respect to whether a crop insurance scheme can be made practical, and they believe that with the information so obtained the chances are that over the greater part of the prairie area crop insurance could in fact be made operative.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in effect since 1939, and there is no question but that it has brought great benefit to the prairie producers. It is an act they all support. It is something they hope the government will continue and expand, but many of them wonder in what direction the government is in fact travelling. Back in 1939 when the legislation was introduced there was a maximum payment of $500 and a minimum comparable payment of $300, plus an additional category that does not apply at this time. Since 1939 there have been tremendous increases in the farmer's cost of production. The minister's own department has published an index in the Economic Annalist based on 1935-39 costs equalling 100. According to the index the cost of production has increased two and a half times since 1939. As a matter of fact, in 1939 the index stood at 99.3 and the latest cost of production index figure is 254.3. Therefore the farmer's cost of production has increased two and a half times within that period.
Anyone who is acquainted at all with the costs of the things farmers have to buy can understand now how this situation has been brought about. One could buy a new one-ton truck in 1939 for $1,000, but a similar truck today would cost approximately $3,000. The best combine that could be purchased in 1939 could be obtained for approximately $2,000. The best combine today costs some $7,000. Therefore the value of the legislation in relation to the farmer's cost of production has gone down very substantially since 1939.
When the suggested amendments become law, if the government does not increase the payments beyond the forecast made this afternoon the value of the new schedule of prairie farm assistance payments for 1957 will be substantially less in purchasing power than the payments of 1939. Notwithstanding the fact that the government has waited 18 years to increase the dollar value of prairie farm assistance payments, the government is


not increasing them by an amount that will restore their value. The government has allowed inflation to chisel away a great part of the purchasing power of prairie farm assistance payments.
I have some figures here on the increased cost of production and the way the value of prairie farm assistance has gone down almost every year since 1939. The government's bill had scarcely been passed in 1939 when the increasing cost of production began to eat away the value of the payments. In 1940, the first year following the passing of the act, the cost of production index rose from 99.3 to 106.8 and the value of the maximum payment under prairie farm assistance dropped in that one year by $35. The next year the cost of production index went up another 10 points and the value of prairie farm assistance dropped $37. The next year the purchasing power went down another $51, and the next year it dropped a further $31. In 1944 it dropped another $11 and in 1945 another $9. In 1946 the value went down $10. In 1947 the cost of production again increased and the purchasing power of this assistance went down another $25. In 1948 it dropped $39, in 1949 another $9, in 1950 a further $7, in 1951 another $20, and in 1952 a further $12. In 1953 there was a small gain of $3 and in 1954 a gain of $1. In 1955 there was a drop of $1, and in 1956, with inflation running wild again, there was a drop of an additional $19.
On the basis of the minister's own cost of production index, in terms of 1939 dollars the $500 maximum prairie farm assistance payment has dropped to $188. What do the government propose to do? They propose to increase the maximum payment per acre from $2.50 to $4 and the maximum total payment from $500 to $800. But $800 today in terms of 1939 purchasing power is only worth $312. Therefore on the basis of the minister's increased payments the new value today is substantially less than it was in 1939. If the minister merely restored the 1939 purchasing power to the maximum prairie farm assistance payment, then according to his own cost of production index the payment would have to be increased from $500 to $1,280, not merely to $800.
So the minister would need to add another $480 to the amount he has presented to the house for prairie farm assistance in 1957 to be worth as much as it was worth in 1939.
With regard to the smaller category, the $300 payment would have to be increased to $760, but the minister is increasing the payment to only $400. Therefore on the basis of his announcement the new rate of payment in the zero to three bushel category will be $360 short of its purchasing power in 1939.

I hope the government will reconsider its proposals. Certainly the very least the government should do is restore the value of prairie farm assistance so the act will be as valuable to the producer as it was in 1939. As a matter of fact, if equity were to be brought to the agricultural industry there should be a much larger increase.
The other day in this house the Prime Minister told us that in order to give to a group of teachers today a salary sufficiently large to take care of the increased cost of living since 1938, and to allow teachers to share in the general increase in production in this country, their salaries would have to be at a level 3i times that of 1938. I suggest to the government that if they were to restore the value of prairie farm assistance and, in addition, were to allow the farmers to gain by the general increase in wealth production in this country, prairie farm assistance should be increased by 3J times over the 1939 level. Instead of introducing a bill to bring about a maximum payment of $800, on that basis it should be $1,750. For the lower payment, instead of being $400 it should be increased to $1,050.
The prairie producers have waited 18 years in order to get from the minister an announcement that, as far as prairie farm assistance is concerned, even with these improvements their position will be worse than it was in 1939. Even with these amendments the purchasing power of the new prairie farm assistance payment will be down about 40 per cent from that of 1939. If this country should have the misfortune of having this government in power for a great many years to come, if they stayed as a government for another 18 years and did with prairie farm assistance what they have done with it in the last 18 years, the producers would then find that the value of the maximum $500 payment of 1939 had become only $193; and if the government should be able to last an additional 18 years, then on the basis of their past 18-year record the $500 value of the 1939 prairie farm assistance payment would be $120.
Is that progress? Is that the best this government can do? Even with the suggestions the minister has made-even when they become law-after prairie farm assistance has been increased the purchasing power will be almost 40 per cent less than it was in 1939. I suggest that as far as prairie farm assistance is concerned the farmer's position in 1939 was not good, and that the $500 payment in 1939 was not enough. I cannot understand why an administration that keeps referring to the great production of the country, the increasing gross national product, should
Prairie Farm Assistance Act say to almost 200,000 producers on the prairies, "As far as prairie farm assistance is concerned we are not going to allow you to have even the same low standard you had in 1939." What they are saying is that after 18 years in office, after bringing forth all the amendments they could consider within an 18-year period, the producers will have to take 40 per cent less in terms of purchasing power than the 1939 prairie farm assistance.
There are other reasons why the assistance should be increased. The price of a bushel of wheat has gone up about 2J times since 1939. I refer to the farm price of high-grade wheat. Therefore the 1 per cent levy has gone up by a similar amount. Hence there are more dollars coming into the fund. There are more dollars coming in because the production has been higher.
In addition to that-and this is something the government has apparently overlooked and I do not believe any other hon. member has yet referred to it-there are fewer farmers on the prairies now than there were in 1939. Hence in any time of widespread crop failure the number of producers who might obtain payments is going down substantially. The 1941 census, which was taken two years after the act went into effect, showed approximately 316,000 producers on the prairies. By 1951 the number of producers had fallen to 248,000, a drop of almost 25 per cent. So now when there is a crop failure there are 25 per cent fewer producers who can obtain prairie farm assistance.
It is true that farms are increasing in size and that fact, to some extent, will compensate for the reduced numbers. But the net effect of the dwindling farm population is to reduce the amount of money paid out in any crop failure year. If figures were available as to the number of producers on the prairies I imagine one would find that since this act first went into effect the number of producers has dropped by at least one-third.
So because of the decreasing value of the payment through the decreasing purchasing power of the dollar; because of the increased contribution by the producers resulting from the increased price of wheat; because there are fewer producers on the prairies than there were in 1939, for all these reasons I suggest that the minister should have further consultation with the cabinet between now and the time the bill is printed and distributed, in order that he may bring in a bill that will restore the value of prairie farm assistance and allow the farmers to share in the growing production of this country.
I placed on the order paper this session a resolution asking that prairie farm assistance be doubled. In that resolution I did not

Prairie Farm Assistance Act go as far as I have gone this evening. In looking over the statements I have made on prairie farm assistance over the years I find that in 1945 I advocated that the payment be $6 per acre. After the government said no to such a proposal year after year I felt that perhaps I should reduce my demand in the hope that the government would move in that direction. So this year I placed on the order paper a resolution asking that prairie farm assistance be doubled. If that were done it would not fully restore the value of prairie farm assistance, it would not in any way allow the farmers to obtain any share of the growing wealth production of this country, but it would certainly be a vast improvement over the suggestions the government has made.
In addition to asking that greater payments be made, I believe there are some other amendments the government should consider. The minister knows very well that under the definitions certain people who paid into the prairie farm assistance fund are unable to obtain awards. The government says that unless a person who is farming has that as his major occupation he is unable to participate in the prairie farm assistance fund. I fully realize the thinking of the government behind that provision, namely that they do not want the public treasury to bonus people who are not full-time farmers and who, perhaps, do not need this additional money.
But it seems to me that with certain changes in farming taking place over the years, the government should take a look at that policy today. I am sure the minister knows, as I know, that there are a great many farmers today who have had to accept some other occupations. They carry on two occupations at the same time, and on the basis of the income they receive farming is a minor occupation, even though the total income they receive from both occupations may not be high. Such a person, even though he contributes to the fund, is not allowed to receive payments.
I know many people in this category, but I have in mind a school teacher by the name of Zach Geib who lived in my little hamlet of Kayville, Sask. and who has quite a large family. He decided to rent a half section of land. He was unfortunate enough to have a crop failure so naturally he applied for prairie farm assistance. He was turned down on the ground that his main occupation was that of school teacher. He paid into the fund, but he was not able to receive any benefits from it. He has decided, therefore, that he cannot afford to stay on the farm and he cannot afford to remain in the teaching


profession, because he is unable to maintain his family on this relatively small income.
Basically I do not think there is anything wrong with having quite a large number of persons on the prairies who engage in farming, but not as their full-time occupation. As I have thought of this problem over the years, it has seemed to me to be basically unjust, basically undemocratic, that you should force a group of people, year after year, to pay into a fund from which, by law, you prevent them receiving any benefit. Some farmers have been paying into the fund for many years, but by law they are prevented from receiving any payments from the fund at a time of crop failure.
I suggest to the minister he might have a look at that regulation, to see whether or not it might be liberalized so that a larger number of persons who are actually farming, who are doing the work themselves, who are paying all their expenses and contributing to the fund, may have an opportunity in time of crop failure of receiving payments from that fund.
I am very pleased that the minister has announced that the bill will be referred to the agriculture committee. A few years ago the minister announced in this house the provisions of a bill under which very substantial areas of crown land on the prairies were to be taken out of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so far as payments were concerned. This bill went to the agriculture committee and, because of the opinions expressed in that committee, the bill was redrafted and large sections of crown land which had been removed from the application of the act were replaced under it.
I believe the minister now should go the whole way and return to the act all crown land, particularly crown lands that have been sold since 1940; land that is good arable land and which no one says should not be in the production of crops. I think people who farm that kind of land or land that was obtained that way are in the same category as the school teacher I have described. They are forced by law to pay into the fund and therefore should be allowed, in certain circumstances, to receive benefits in the same way any other farmer may.
The people on the prairies believe the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a good act. They think it is helpful, and they are hopeful that the government may be able to further amend the proposed bill so the value of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in 1957 may be raised at least to the level of 1939.

I think the resolution under discussion is particularly important, because it could form the nucleus of

much-needed crop insurance legislation. I say this because the farm organizations in Canada have envisaged the adoption by a government of this country of an agricultural policy. We in this group have pressed for the adoption of an agricultural policy, but the government has continuously ignored our requests. I bring this point out to keep the matter in its proper perspective because after all, Mr. Chairman, the P.F.A.A. is intended as a relief measure to help those who are unable to make a livelihood as the result of a disaster of nature. We call it the dried out bonus in my area of Saskatchewan, but it has been extended to cover other things such as hail or flood or other causes of crop losses.
I do not think we want to look on this P.F.A.A. as a measure to make up for the shortcomings of the government in not introducing an agricultural policy. It has been pointed out by members in this debate that the amount paid under P.F.A.A. is really very small indeed. In introducing the measure the Minister of Agriculture stated that its function was to allow the farmer to pay for groceries. I do not know at what store the minister is buying his groceries, nor do I know the size of his family, but the $500 which the act presently provides would not buy many groceries, nor would the $800 that the amendment will provide. I would relate this to the position of the old age pensioner who, as has been pointed out in the house, cannot possibly survive on a pension of $40 per month or $480 per year. Then how could we expect a man with a family to pay for groceries and pay some of his other expenses with $800 a year?
As the hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out, the inflationary trend which this government has nurtured has robbed the farmer of the benefits he would get under the act. Coming back to my point of relating it to agricultural policy, I think if we get to the stage where we have a government in power that is dedicated to the welfare of the people of Canada, one that will introduce a comprehensive agricultural policy based on the recommendations of farm organizations, an agricultural policy that will guarantee a reasonable standard of living and will give the family farm a parity of income with other occupations, our need for P.F.A.A. as such will be diminished.
I say it will be diminished, because under an agricultural program which would give security to the livestock man, the poultry producer and the fruit grower, as my friend the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary pointed out, there would be less necessity for him to depend on the one-crop basis. The 82715-92
Prairie Farm Assistance Act areas in western Canada that have received the crop failure bonus are those areas which in all probability should be devoted to ranching or diversified farming.
If this is true, and if the government introduced the kind of agricultural policy it should introduce, a farmer would not be trying to grow wheat on land which is really suited for ranching or some other function. As it presently is, with the guarantee of price under the Canadian wheat board, we find that the farmer has some security for his produce. He knows what he is going to receive in the crop year. The same cannot be said of many aspects of the agricultural industry.
The minister might point out that there are floor prices under eggs and hogs, but those floor prices have no relationship to the cost of production. They are put on an ad hoc basis, just slipped in under the market price, and I suspect that if the market prices slipped down the floor prices would slip down right on top of them. We do not really have the security which would allow a farmer to organize an enterprise on an efficient basis.
The minister has stated that he has been a very strong advocate of the South Saskatchewan river irrigation project. I would point out that an irrigation project such as this, which has been requested for the last 30 years by the farmers of Saskatchewan, would do a great deal to reduce the expenditures of the prairie farm assistance administration, because it would remove a vast area of land from the risky business of wheat production and transform it into an irrigated area.
The same is certainly true in other areas, as the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, areas which should be diversified and should have their production base broadened so they can be taken out of the risky field of grain production. The purpose of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be to provide a nucleus for this over-all system of crop insurance which should accompany an agricultural policy. If you have an agricultural policy on a nation-wide basis the one factor that will be missing will be security in case of crop failure or disaster. The P.F.A.A. could certainly provide the nucleus for legislation which would complement an agricultural policy. It should be extended to all areas, so that if through disaster a farmer suffered financial hardship he would be buttressed by the crop insurance program, which would provide him with a reasonable standard of living or at least allow him to meet expenses during such trying times. I am certain that such a scheme would be readily acceptable to all parts of the economy.
Certain objections which have been voiced to the P.F.A.A. are based on the participation
145Q

Prairie Farm, Assistance Act of farmers through the contributions they make, with a limited opportunity of receiving any benefit from it. A nation-wide crop insurance program would certainly remove this criticism. Until the government sees fit to introduce an over-all agricultural policy which would take advantage of the survey of land use that is currently being made in the other place, we have to content ourselves with the legislation that is presently on the books. It is good legislation and well meaning, but as I have pointed out we should not try to have the P.F.A.A. take the place of an agricultural policy. The P.F.A.A. is emergency assistance. Let us therefore try to expand the P.F.A.A. so it will play an effective role in providing crop insurance. Let us follow the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, who said we should make certain that the payments made under P.F.A.A. are sufficient to meet the needs.
In view of the extremely low quotas in certain points of western Canada I sometimes think P.F.A.A. payments should be made to farmers who are unable to market their quotas. I say that in a rather jocular vein because that is not the purpose of the act, but it is based on the principle of providing stop-gap assistance to those who are not in a position to assist themselves. Consideration should be given to enlarging the application of the act, which should be on an individual basis.
I realize the administrative difficulties involved in that but if we are going to look to the P.F.A.A. as a means of providing assistance to unfortunate farmers who are suffering crop failure or disaster through no fault of their own, the act must be extended on an individual basis. It is small comfort to a man to be living just outside of a township that qualifies, when he has been wiped out by the same hail storm that enabled the township to qualify. It is small comfort indeed for him to have his crop completely wiped out, when he realizes that there are some individuals in the township who reap some benefit and who qualified by virtue of the whole township qualifying. Those are the factors that will create dissension among farmers in the operation of the act, and these problems will be resolved only when the act is put on an individual basis which will take care of such situations.
I do not think I need to say anything more. The government should be well aware of the need for an agricultural policy. We in this group have certainly expressed that view on many occasions, and farm organizations in presenting their briefs to the government have stated a similar opinion on numerous occasions. Since the P.F.A.A. was originated I think
fMr. Argue.]
very little relief has been paid out by any of the provinces which have received this form of aid. And when we discuss the deduction of 1 per cent, or whatever it will be, as the farmers' contribution thereto, I think the provinces should give consideration to what it formerly cost them, and what it would be costing them throughout the years if the P.F.A.A. were not in existence.
All of us remember those years on relief. Crop insurance and P.F.A.A. and crop failure assistance are very much in the minds of every one of us in the southwestern portions of the province. Thus we are naturally interested in crop insurance in the United States or wherever else it may be in operation. Even to this day, however, if my figures are correct, only between 20 and 25 per cent of the people who are eligible for coverage in the United States are, in fact, protected by this crop insurance policy.
In practice there are limitations to the effectiveness of such a scheme. Where the need is greatest, people are not in a position to pay the premiums required. An eligible farmer who is in a position to take advantage of crop insurance can benefit thereby, it is true, but there are too many situations in which farmers are not eligible because they live in areas where the risks are too great. Their applications are rejected because high risks are not eligible for participation.
Below me, in Montana, the scheme operates on a basis of 12 counties in the way such a scheme might be operated on the basis of municipalities in Canada. Counties which have a low yield are eliminated. Applications for coverage are screened in two operations. First of all the land in respect of which an application is made is classified. If the land is very poor and has a record of crop failure, the application is rejected. Second, the record of the individual farmer is examined. Those who are considered to be poor risks are declared ineligible for participation. The result is that over 5 per cent of the farmers in 810 counties in the U. S. are not eligible for insurance.
There is no eligibility qualification under the P.F.A.A. There is no distinction as between farmers, and there is no distinction as between land. So it would appear to me that though a crop insurance program would be more favourable, no method has yet been devised whereby it could be made applicable to as great a number of farmers as P.F.A.A.
Again, crop insurance operates in the United States not by way of ensuring a profit to an individual farmer but merely on a sustaining basis with regard to the crop

that is necessary to maintain him. That is the amount for which he can insure. As I say, the system has its limitations. It requires investigation and study, and in the meantime we have the best system here that has yet been devised in any country in the world to sustain us until such time as a better system, or a real system of crop insurance, can be instituted.
There has been some question in the minds of some of the provinces-perhaps Manitoba can be mentioned-as to whether they are satisfied with the situation, inasmuch as some people claim that they are paying more toward the P.F.A.A. than they have received in crop failure payments. I would remind them that they have other compensations to which they should give a little consideration. They should remember that the bulk of our wheat is sold on the markets of the world and commands a premium because it has a high protein content.
In the United States, farmers who grow high protein wheat receive benefits for doing so. If they have more than 16 per cent of protein in their wheat they are eligible for a 40 cent premium in the mills of Minneapolis and elsewhere. In the southwestern part of our province and in other areas of Saskatchewan we grow a wheat with a high protein content. We normally do that, and that affects the price which all farmers in western Canada receive for their wheat, because an individual who grows a wheat of high protein content receives no greater benefit from it than an individual who grows a wheat of lower protein content. I think that latter situation is more prevalent in Manitoba than elsewhere, so the farmers in Manitoba receive some benefit which would not be theirs if, as a result of the elimination of the P.F.A.A., the farmers who grow high protein content wheat demanded that they should receive compensation in respect of the higher quality wheat which they produce.
As I say, factors like this enter into the situation. I think it should also be taken into consideration that relief payments by the provinces have been practically eliminated as a result of the payment of millions of dollars into those areas through the P.F.A.A. There has been some discussion today with regard to government insurance and the extent to which it is applicable to the provinces, and some have advocated that the P.F.A.A. be on an individual basis.
I agree we could originate a policy along these lines and yet not interfere with the situation, and I would suggest that if the province of Saskatchewan, which has had the burden of relief lifted from it for so many years, would contribute an additional dollar an acre
Prairie Farm Assistance Act on land in the lower category of P.F.A.A. payments and a smaller amount in the other categories, that would automatically put them into the crop insurance business.
Perhaps, as a result, a method could be devised more suitable to the situation, something which would be more acceptable to the people in that area. For example, payments would not be in the form of compensation as relief but, rather, in the form of a subvention which would enable them to extend or continue their operations without having to offset the expenses of one year against the hope of a crop in the following year.
We know the value of the dollar is not the same as it was in 1939. We have heard it said by hon. members on my left time and time again that the present-day value is only 60 cents, or 40 cents, or whatever value they may choose to place on it. I have here the minutes of a meeting which was held in southwestern Saskatchewan on November 28, 1949. That was a year of crop failure, and the farmers held mass meetings at that time. Many hon. members will remember them. The preamble to one of the resolutions moved to urge an increase in crop failure payments reads:
Whereas the purchasing power of the dollar is only one-third of what it was in 1939-
If that preamble is right; if it is correct that in 1949 the dollar was only worth one-third of what it was worth in 1939, then the value of the dollar must be increasing, because I have not heard anyone in these later days say that the dollar is only worth one-third of what it was in 1939. It has been pointed out that the purchasing power of the dollar is not so great and that crop failure payments should increase with the growth in wealth of the people of Canada.
Having regard to the financial position of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the fact that they are now receiving $30 million to $33 million under dominion-provincial agreements and other benefits from the federal government that are increasing each year, I think those provinces could give some consideration to the farmers and contribute that one additional dollar or more if they wished. I believe they would be opening the door or putting the foot in the door to further association under agreements between the federal and provincial governments, and would be contributing to a more stable situation and a better method of keeping the farmers operating, because that is all this assistance does at the present time, if it goes that far. They would be contributing to a more beneficial situation in southwestern Saskatchewan and all the other areas where the farmers from time to time have to fall

Prairie Farm Assistance Act back upon the federal government and other governments to assist them in periods of adversity.
Together with other hon. members I should like to commend the government for this great step forward. I hope we will never lessen our initiative and our efforts to place the farmers of western Canada in a position so that when difficulties surround them they will know their governments are ready and willing to come to their rescue.

Mr. Chairman, it is indeed fortunate that this legislation should come before the house at a time when so many representatives of the prairie farmers happen to be in the capital. While recognizing the drawbacks that are inherent in any such scheme, I should merely like to draw the attention of the minister to certain things and ask him to comment on what steps the government may intend to take to provide a similar plan of assistance for the farmers of the maritime provinces.
Our farmers have to compete with United States products. United States turkeys, for instance, are selling in Campbellton, New Brunswick, much cheaper than Canadian turkeys can be produced and sold. United States potatoes are being brought into New Brunswick under a protective tariff system and being shipped to Montreal with the benefit of preferred freight rates for a much lower cost than in the case of our own potatoes. While our farmers cannot sell their milk, we are importing into New Brunswick 1,500 carloads of milk a year.
I wish to draw the attention of the minister to these problems, and I will have occasion to do so more particularly in the future. I request in all sincerity that steps be taken by the government to provide for the maritime farmer the same advantages the government provides for farmers in the western provinces. I realize that in the past the agricultural policy of the government has been in many cases to favour the prairie farmer. I have always felt that under all these schemes the maritime farmer has been neglected. I feel that the minister will be more than anxious to see that steps are taken to put the maritime farmer in the same trading position as the government is placing the western wheat farmer.
It is most discouraging to visit our farms in northern New Brunswick and see that the farmers are unable to sell their potatoes at a price which will compensate them for the cost of growing them. It is most unfortunate and distressing to visit our farms in northern New Brunswick and find the farmers in a position where they cannot sell their dairy products. I think all members from the
[Mr. Studer.l
maritime provinces, regardless of party politics, whether they be Liberal or Conservative, are in agreement and will all agree that the maritime farmer is the forgotten farmer of Canada.
This is an anomaly which should not exist in a country such as Canada. Possibly the reasons for the plight of the maritime farmers go far beyond the limitations the government has set with regard to the measures it may take to help the farmers of the maritime provinces. Nevertheless I believe the minister will agree that a chain is no stronger than its weakest link, and if in one section of the country we have farmers who are unable to make a living in whatever type of farming they are engaged-and that is the case in northern New Brunswick-I am sure the minister is prepared to take steps to alleviate the condition of the farmers of the maritime provinces.
It is discouraging to see our potato farmers up against a wall for three years in a row and unable to sell their potatoes at a price that will permit them to buy seed for the following year. They must sell at a price which does not permit them to repay their bank loans, and they are having more and more difficulty making such loans, obtained in order to buy seed for the next year's crop. It is discouraging to see our farmers having to kill their cows because they cannot sell the milk. It is discouraging to see how United States farmers just across the border are placed by this very government in a more advantageous position than our own Canadian farmers in northern New Brunswick and the maritime provinces.
I feel that the minister will recognize these problems. They are too serious to joke about. I believe it is not too late for steps to be taken to make sure that the farmer of the maritime provinces is put in the same trading position as the farmer of the west. I realize that the minister may get up and cite chapter and verse going back over many years of history, but the stark fact is that years ago 75 to 100 carloads of potatoes were shipped to Cuba each year; then merely because we put an embargo on their sugar Cuba retaliated by cancelling practically all their orders for New Brunswick potatoes, and now they take from New Brunswick farmers less than one carload of potatoes a year.

In the first place, I quite agree with my hon. friend from the maritimes that he may be a little bit discouraged in listening to what has been said in criticism of the many dollars we are spending in some places, and maybe he is feeling that probably he should raise some criticism because there has not been that much spent in some other direction. That is entirely assistance to persons who are living east of Fort William and west of the mountains. Then I have said in this house on one or two occasions previously-and I repeat it now, and I do not say it by way of criticism of those who received it-that those who have received the highest returns of any farmers in Canada throughout the years are the apple growers of the maritimes. Certain suggestions have been made that we should have crop insurance, and an attempt has been made in the Saskatchewan report to indicate that I have always thought this was crop insurance and have always called it crop insurance. My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia has even gone so far as to quote from the record as contained in the provincial royal commission's report to suggest that. But I am sure hon. members of the house recall perfectly well that every time I have discussed this question in the house I have argued that it is not crop insurance. He-

In other words, I am saying it is not our responsibility to bring in crop insurance but it is the responsibility of the province. That is in 1939. We were discussing the question of the levy. Some questions were asked in the house, and it was intimated that that was something which indicated that there was an element of insurance in it. I simply go on to answer that question by using the same terms that were used by the individual who was making the criticism. But I do not think it is necessary, either in the house or outside of it, for me to try to prove that I have never at any time maintained that this is crop insurance. I certainly have not. I have always maintained that we did not have authority to bring in crop insurance, and we have never attempted to introduce it.
I quite agree with some hon. members that it would be a good thing for Canada if we had crop insurance, but I do not agree with those who say that we can lead in bringing in crop insurance. Every authority I have ever consulted in connection with the matter says we cannot do that. But I do not know that there is anything in the constitution or anywhere else that prevents us assisting some province that does want to bring in insurance. We may be able to consider giving some assistance in connection with it; but to say that under our constitution we can lead in bringing in insurance is contrary to all the advice I have ever had in connection with it.
I think if we want to discuss that question at some other time it is quite proper to do so, but it is not part of this measure. We are not attempting to bring in crop insurance, and we are not attempting to argue against those who think crop insurance would be a good thing. The only question I would raise in connection with what has been said tonight with regard to it has to do with the United States system. There is no one who has ever argued that the United States system would do for our farmers what prairie

farm assistance does. The farmers of the United States do not argue that. As a matter of fact, when they discuss prairie farm assistance and compare it with their own system they indicate they have nothing to compare with our system to take care of farmers who may be suffering from drought conditions or some other condition.
In the United States they simply set up a fund of $100 million which the farmers are supposed to pay back some day. Then a system is set up under which they think the farmers will be able to pay it back. In order to set up that system they do exactly what has been said here tonight by a number of members, they zone the country and say you can have insurance in this area but you cannot have it in that area. They say that very definitely. In other words they take a section of the country in which the farmers can afford to pay for insurance and say all right, you can have it. You only get it if you write it up. You do not get it automatically, as you get the benefits from this measure. An agent comes out and tries to write up the insurance, just the same as they do in this country for hail insurance, fire insurance, life insurance or any other kind of insurance. It is only the farmers who think they can afford to pay the premium who have the insurance.
As I recall the figures in the Saskatchewan report, they indicate that some 26 per cent of the eligible producers in the United States participated. There is a considerable percentage of them not affected by that legislation at all. Most of those just across the line from North Dakota in Saskatchewan would be the people who benefit from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Some of them may be on land that is not quite as good as other land; some of them may have suffered from serious drought conditions; some of them may have suffered from rust, grasshoppers or any of these afflictions that cause loss to farmers. Under this legislation they draw on the fund automatically. It is not a question of having looked into the future and written up an insurance policy, and therefore drawing money. The money is paid to them automatically.
The hon. member for Kindersley was very eloquent in connection with the matter of paying store bills and so on. I would remind him of the fact that the very area from which he comes draws as heavily from this fund as any section in western Canada. The people are in that position because they have been farming land that is comparatively dry. I have been out in that district. I was out there in 1910 when they were homesteading and when you could see the gophers sitting up in the oat crop. Their heads were 82715-93
Prairie Farm Assistance Act higher than the oat crop when it was headed out. It was certainly dry enough that the people wanted to be helped.
Then I was back there later, in 1915, when I saw 130,000 bushels of wheat piled in one heap waiting for an elevator to be built so it could be put in cars and shipped out. I was back again later when the people were back in debt as deeply as they had been when they completed settling on their farms, and they were asking for help in order to get through that difficult period. I was back again last year and saw the wheat piled in the same areas and on the same farms as I saw it piled away back in 1915. This is an area in which they have their ups and downs. They have a drought in one period and good crops in another period, and they try to average it out over the years. This legislation helps them stay there and do that; it helps people of that kind who are spread over a very considerable section of the prairie country to remain and produce.
This is all the legislation is intended to do. It is not intended that it should be crop insurance or settle all the difficulties of the prairie farmers or the farmers in all parts of Canada. We have other methods whereby we do settle a lot of their difficulties. I only want to say that up to now we have spent 10 times more looking after the farmers of Canada than any other government we have had, Liberal or Tory. This is not a bad record for a government that is not supposed to have an agricultural policy at all. We have a pretty fair agricultural policy. The fact is there is not anyone over the last 21 years who has been able to produce a policy that would persuade the people of Canada that they ought to change from this policy. Our policy is fairly good, and it stands up alongside the policies of others.
The hon. member from New Brunswick was talking about conditions in the United States. The price of butter is higher in this country; the price of eggs is higher in this country, and the price of nearly everything is higher in this country. The one thing that is not higher in this country than it is in the United States is wheat, but our wheat sells for a higher price on the market in Liverpool than United States wheat. The same is true of any of the other markets where wheat is sold. We are not so badly off when compared to other people as my friends would have us believe. I do not mean to intimate that the farmers are as well off as they ought to be. However, this act does not make them any worse off, and I urge that the resolution be passed so we can get the legislation introduced.

1. Section 6(c) of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act being Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. chapter 213, provides,
Where the board has determined that an area is eligible for award and a rectangular block of sections of land outside such area having an area of not less than one-half a township is determined by the board to have an average yield of eight bushels of wheat or less per acre such block of sections of land is eligible for award as though it were a complete township.
The rural municipality of Oakland submits that due to the usual irregularity of the locations of the crop damage and/or failure, this section does not give relief to many farmers who may suffer crop damage and/ or failure but who may not be located in the rectangular block as provided by this section and respectfully request that this subsection be amended to read:
That section 6(c) be amended by striking out the word "rectangular" where it appears in the second line thereof and substituting therefor the word "irregular" and by striking out the words "one-half township"
where they appear in the fourth line thereof and substituting therefor the words "six sections".
2.	Section 3(2B) of the said act provides, If the average yield of wheat in the
township is found by the board to be more than four and not more than eight bushels per acre the award shall be $1.50 per acre and
The municipality respectfully submits that with the increased price of farm machinery and equipment and the increased cost of operating a farm the rate should be increased to bring it in line with the maximum provided in the 1939 act and respectfully request that this subsection be amended to read,
That section 3(2B) be amended by striking out the words "$1.50" where they appear in the fourth line thereof and substituting therefor the words "$3.00".
3.	Section 3(2c) of the said act provides, If the average yield of wheat in the
township is found by the board to be not more than four bushels per acre the award shall be $2.50 per acre.
The municipality respectfully submits that with the increased price of farm machinery and equipment and the increased cost of operating a farm the rate should be increased to bring it in line with the maximum provided in the 1939 act and respectfully request that this subsection be amended to read,
That section 3(2c) be amended by striking out the words "$2.50" where they appear in the third line thereof and substituting therefor the words "$5.00".
4.	Section 3 (3b) of the said act provides, "With respect to more than two hundred
acres of cultivated land of the farm or" The municipality respectfully submits that the present day farmer has become a large land owner and is continually expanding and as such contributes that much more and the municipality respectfully submits that this subsection be amended to read,
That the section 3 (3b) be amended by striking out the word "two" where it appears in the first line thereof and substituting therefor the word "three".
5.	The municipality respectfully submits that there are cases where the farmer is receiving assistance under this act for cultivated land which is not self supporting and for this reason the purpose of the act is being

exploited and respectfully submits that there be a subsection added to section 3 of the said act restricting any award under this act to farmers whose lands affected are not self supporting and to define and classify the type of land which will be eligible for assistance.
6.	The municipality respectfully submits that due to the usual irregularity of the locations of the crop damage by hail that any individual farmer in any area that suffers loss of crop through hail be qualified for assistance under the said act provided he comes within the provisions of section 3 of the said act and respectfully submits that there be a subsection added to section 6 of the said act to provide that if a farmer or a group of farmers lose their crop or a portion thereof by hail then the individual farmers
Prairie Farm Assistance Act in that area should be eligible for assistance under the said act.
7.	The municipality respectfully submits that in determining the assistance to be given to farmers under this act consideration should be given not only to the yield and grade of the grain but also to the loss in expenses to the farmer in salvaging his crop and respectfully submits that there be a subsection added to section 3 of the said act to provide for assistance for such loss.
8.	The municipality respectfully submits that when the department pays the farmer the assistance to which he is entitled to under the said act that the department attach to each cheque a statement showing how the department and/or board arrived at the amount awarded to each farmer.
Wednesday, February 20, 1957
